members.researchInterests: The overarching theme of his research is to make information ecosystems and technologies more pluralistic, so they are inclusive of voices that have been historically marginalized. To this end, he develops quantitative measures that measure representational gaps in diverse contexts, from entrenched biases in conversational AI systems, to content gaps in large-scale information management systems, to representational gaps in news coverage. These measures are informed by studies and methods from humanistic inquiry, including critical discourse analysis, ethnographic fieldwork, and archival research, to ensure maximal ecological validity. His work is equally dedicated to a high degree of construct validity, grounded in my training in machine learning and data science.

members.bio: Ramaravind is a Ph.D. candidate in the Faculty of Information, a graduate fellow of the Data Sciences Institute (DSI), a graduate fellow of the Centre for Ethics, and a graduate affiliate of the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society (SRI) at the University of Toronto. He is co-advised by Prof. Ishtiaque Ahmed and Prof. Shion Guha. He is a member of the Department of Computer Science's ThirdSpace research group, the Dynamics Graphics Project lab, and the iSchool's Human-Centered Data Science Lab.
members.researchInterests: Ramaravind studies AI safety through the lens of the people who actually build systems with AI models. He unpacks the often implicit choices practitioners make in how they frame safety problems and build data and model workflows around them. Building on this, he develops reflective frameworks that help practitioners examine their safety choices and computational methods that make that reflection actionable. Together, these support practitioners in making AI safety decisions more reflectively and with greater nuance at critical stages of their practice. His research sits at the intersection of HCI, NLP, and philosophy, drawing on user studies of how practitioners reason and on informal logic and argumentation theories.

members.bio: Sheza Munir is a PhD student in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto, advised by Dr. Ishtiaque Ahmed. She holds a Master’s in Information from the University of Michigan and studied Computer Science at LUMS. Her work focuses on how disagreement is preserved or erased in human-AI systems, from the data that trains models to the agents that act and negotiate. She is a Junior Fellow at Massey College, a Research Fellow at the Collective Intelligence Project and a Research Associate at the MIT Global Humanities Initiative.
members.title: PhD Student
members.researchInterests: Munir’s research sits at the intersection of NLP, HCI, and the social sciences. She studies how disagreement is managed, and often lost, when humans and AI agents have to reach a shared answer: who gets to label, how lived experience shapes judgment, how labels and preferences are aggregated, and how agents handle conflict with people and with each other. She builds methods and evaluations that keep plural perspectives, and the reasons behind them, alive from annotation to decision.

members.bio: Dipto Das is a postdoctoral researcher whose work bridges AI, algorithmic accountability, and socio-technical systems. He examines how AI systems and online platforms shape decision-making, public discourse, and identity across varied cultural contexts. His research covers AI governance, context-sensitive fairness measures, and cultural/political dimensions of AI usage.
members.researchInterests: Dipto's research covers three threads: Governing (studying policies, impact assessments, AI registries and procurement for accountability), Evaluating (context-sensitive fairness measures and benchmarks for low-resource languages), and Situating (cultural/political dimensions of AI usage, including identity, moderation, and diaspora practices).

professor.researchInterests: Ishtiaque's current research focuses on AI safety, AI governance, AI policy, ethical and responsible AI design, and human–AI interaction. He designs AI tools and services aimed at addressing global challenges in health, sustainability, and peace in a responsible and accountable manner. His work critically examines the ethical foundations of AI systems and explores community-based, participatory approaches to AI development. His research is primarily published in HCI venues such as CHI, CSCW, FAccT, ICTD, DIS, and COMPASS, as well as AI venues including ACL, EACL, ECIR, AAAI, and WWW.
professor.title: Associate Professor
professor.bio: Ishtiaque Ahmed is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto and serves as Associate Director of the Knowledge Media Design Institute (KMDI). He is also affiliated with the University of Toronto's iSchool, Data Sciences Institute, School of the Environment, School of Cities, Institute of Health Emergencies and Pandemics, Acceleration Consortium, and Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society. In addition, he serves on the University of Toronto's Research Ethics Board (REB) and AI Task Force. Beyond the University of Toronto, he has served as the National AI Consultant for Bangladesh with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and is a member of the MIT Global Humanities Initiative.

topics.title: Migration & Diaspora
topics.summary: How immigrants, refugees, and diasporas navigate — and are governed by — digital infrastructures.
topics.metaDescription: How immigrants, refugees, and diasporas navigate — and are governed by — digital infrastructures.

cover.alt: Figure from "Memory through Design: Supporting Cultural Identity for Immigrants through a Paper-Based Home Drafting Tool"

topics.intro:
Digital infrastructures now shape almost every part of migration, from sending money home to proving who you are in a new country. We study how immigrants, refugees, and diasporas from the Global South navigate these systems, and design with them for fairer alternatives.

Our work looks at the politics as well as the practicalities: how diasporas organize for change at home, how borders reappear inside data systems, and how communities build informal networks of trust when formal systems fail them.

sections.heading: Diasporas and Transnational Politics
sections.body:
During Bangladesh's 2024 quota-reform movement, non-resident Bangladeshis used social platforms and remittance flows to challenge state authority. [How do the Global South Diasporas Mobilize for Transnational Political Change?](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791792) (CHI 2026, Best Paper Honorable Mention) traces the phases of their collective action — from technology-mediated engagement and rapid network building to a strategic remittance boycott and adaptive responses to surveillance and information blackouts — and introduces the idea of "diasporic superposition". A companion study documents how the ten-day nationwide internet shutdown during the movement affected the rights of Bangladeshis living abroad ([Internet Disconnection as a Risk to Cross-Border Human Rights](https://doi.org/10.1145/3706599.3720245)).

Borders also persist inside data systems. Drawing on interviews with 32 immigrants in Canada, [Data Migration in HCI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790605) (CHI 2026) shows how credit bureaus, credential evaluators, healthcare databases, and immigration portals gatekeep immigrants' civic rights, and how community-mediated informal networks help people make their data legitimate in a new country. Related work examines AI in immigration decision-making through [Canadian parliamentary discourse](https://doi.org/10.1353/ces.2025.a989105) and [how information retrieval systems construct and amplify immigration narratives](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-21324-2_36).

sections.heading: Infrastructures of Support for Immigrants
sections.body:
When global politics cut communities off from formal financial platforms, people build their own infrastructures. Our three-month ethnography with the Iranian community in Toronto, [Money Whispers](https://doi.org/10.1145/3411764.3445065) (CHI 2021), documented the financial loss, fear, uncertainty, and privacy breaches involved in sending money home, and the informal workarounds that make it possible. With the community, we then co-designed [Kabootar](https://doi.org/10.1145/3555109) (CSCW 2022), a community-based FinTech application that matches senders and receivers of money across borders.

More recently, we have studied Iranian immigrant nonprofits. [Artificial Intelligence at the Margins](https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3812939) (DIS 2026, Best Paper Honorable Mention) shows how legitimacy barriers, capacity gaps, and ethical dilemmas create a cycle of infrastructural immobility — one that generative AI risks deepening. Working with practitioners, we designed [AMINA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30084) (GROUP 2027), an inclusive and accountable AI assistant for immigrant nonprofits. We also follow immigrants' emotional and informational trajectories in Reddit communities over time.

sections.heading: Refugees, Displacement, and Memory
sections.body:
Research on refugees often stops at immediate needs. Our two-year ethnography with Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, [Infrastructuring Hope](https://doi.org/10.1145/3392561.3394640) (ICTD 2020), looks instead at solidarity, leadership, negotiation, and the hopes that shape long-term settlement. We have also studied the everyday lives and ICT use of internally displaced people in northern Iraq ([Exile Within Borders](https://doi.org/10.1145/3338103.3338104)), and how humanitarian workers supported refugees and asylum seekers in Turkey at a distance during COVID-19 ([A Matter of Time](https://doi.org/10.1145/3579455)).

Migration is also about memory and identity. [Memory through Design](https://doi.org/10.1145/3313831.3376636) (CHI 2020, Best Paper Honorable Mention) introduced a paper-based drafting tool through which newcomers express the cultural values of their homes. Stepping back, [A Decade of International Migration Research in HCI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3490555) (ToCHI 2022) surveys 282 publications and interviews 11 researchers to chart how the field has evolved and where it should go next.

topics.summary: Designing with faith, local knowledge, and traditional ways of seeing — beyond Western scientific rationality.

topics.intro:
Much of computing assumes a secular, Western, scientifically rational user. For many people in the Global South, faith, tradition, and local knowledge shape how they make sense of information, technology, and the world.

We take these practices seriously as sources of design insight — studying religious media, rural visual and performative storytelling, and beliefs that sit outside scientific rationality — and build technologies that support interfaith and intercultural understanding.

sections.heading: Religion, Faith, and Technology
sections.body:
Religious values shape how people live, communicate, and care for the world around them. [Religion and Sustainability](https://doi.org/10.1145/3415199) (CSCW 2020) draws lessons for sustainable computing from Islamic religious communities, challenging persuasive design's narrow economic worldview. A nine-month ethnography of Islamic sermons shared online, [Putting The Waz on the Social Media](https://doi.org/10.1145/3491102.3502006) (CHI 2022), examines how digital sermons build an online religious counterpublic, while [Situating Public Speaking](https://doi.org/10.1145/3512911) (CSCW 2022) questions the idea of a universal set of public-speaking skills. During the pandemic, we also wrote about [religious and parareligious responses to COVID-19](https://doi.org/10.1145/3440926) in rural Bangladesh.

Because a lack of interfaith communication can breed prejudice and conflict, we designed [Cohabitant](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642821) (CHI 2024), a virtual reality application that promotes interfaith learning and empathy.

sections.heading: Local Ways of Seeing and Telling
sections.body:
Data visualization rests on two centuries of conventions that may not reflect how many audiences convey information. [Communicating Consequences](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581149) (CHI 2023) contrasts rural traditional visual culture with contemporary data visualization, arguing that understanding traditional practices is needed to build richer, more accessible data narratives. Earlier, Seeing in Context (CSCW 2020) documented traditional visual communication practices in rural Bangladesh.

In a ten-month ethnography in three villages, [Embodying Facts, Figures, and Faiths](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790387) (CHI 2026) studied how communities use entertainment and cultural performance to tell serious stories with data. And [Community Voice as Data](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581458) (CHI 2023) explores how participatory videos can bring communities' own voices into international program development.

sections.heading: Postcolonial Computing: Belief, Luck, and Memory
sections.body:
For many people, especially in the Global South, witchcraft, sorcery, and other occult practices are primary means of seeking health, wealth, and happiness. Building on an eight-month ethnography in six villages, [Witchcraft and HCI](https://doi.org/10.1145/3290605.3300586) (CHI 2019) brings these practices into conversation with postcolonial computing. [Chasing Luck](https://doi.org/10.1145/3411764.3445047) (CHI 2021) shows how villagers combine statistical probability, faith, hunch, and cultural norms in online betting, and [Purdah, Amanah, and Gheebat](https://doi.org/10.1145/3460112.3471957) (COMPASS 2021) shows how Islamic values shape notions of privacy.

We also design for remembrance and cultural exchange. [Politics of the Past](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642496) (CHI 2024) studies how migrant families navigate history through memory and postmemory, and [Be Our Guest](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3581005) (CHI 2023) is an augmented reality application that invites users into homes from different cultures to foster intercultural exchange.

topics.intro:
Online platforms are where many people in the Global South meet, organize, and get their news — and where they face harassment, hate, and misinformation. Mainstream moderation is built largely around Western, secular values and well-resourced languages.

We study how harms are experienced by women, religious and ethnic minorities, and other marginalized users, build detection resources for low-resource languages, and design moderation that draws on community values.

sections.heading: Harassment, Gender, and Justice
sections.body:
Women in the Global South often seek justice for online harassment by sharing screenshots as evidence — evidence that is frequently challenged for its authenticity. Based on a survey of 91 and interviews with 43 Bangladeshi victims, we built [Unmochon](https://doi.org/10.1145/3411764.3445154) (CHI 2021, Best Paper Honorable Mention), a tool for collecting trustworthy evidence of harassment on Facebook Messenger. Earlier, we studied [harassment on anonymous social media in Bangladesh](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287098.3287107) (ICTD 2019).

We have examined who participates in movements like #MeToo and why many do not, in both [Bangladesh](https://doi.org/10.1145/3375195) (GROUP 2020) and [India](https://doi.org/10.1145/3449185) (CSCW 2021). In a conservative society where talking about sex is taboo, [ShishuShurokkha](https://doi.org/10.1145/3491102.3517543) (CHI 2022) takes a transformative-justice approach to combating child sexual abuse.

sections.heading: Hate Speech, Misinformation, and Polarization
sections.body:
Reliable detection is especially hard in low-resource languages. [LLM-Based Multi-Task Bangla Hate Speech Detection](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.1565/) (ACL 2026) detects the type, severity, and target of hate speech in Bangla, and [POLAR](https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.1433/) (ACL 2026 Findings) is a benchmark of over 110K instances in 22 languages for studying online polarization across cultures and events.

We also study the people behind the data. [Combating Misinformation in Bangladesh](https://doi.org/10.1145/3415201) (CSCW 2020) examines the roles of journalists, fact-checkers, and users; [The Politics of Fear](https://doi.org/10.1145/3686926) (CSCW 2024) documents the experiences of religious minority communities on social media; and Combating Islamophobia (TSC 2023) designs for compromise, community, and harmony in mitigating harmful content.

sections.heading: Community-Centred Moderation
sections.body:
As moderation increasingly relies on large language models, we ask whether these systems can recognize culturally insensitive speech toward historically underrepresented communities. [Mod-Guide](https://doi.org/10.1145/3811242.3819096) (COMPASS 2026) is an LLM-based moderation feedback system built for this purpose, and [Argument-Based Consistency in Toxicity Explanations](https://aclanthology.org/2026.eacl-findings.1/) (EACL 2026 Findings) evaluates how LLMs reason about toxicity, not just whether they detect it.

Community values matter too. A [civics-oriented study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3700794.3700802) (ICTD 2024) shows how intersectional identities shape Indigenous and women users' experiences of hate speech; a three-year rural ethnography, [Toleration Factors](https://doi.org/10.1145/3572334.3572378) (ICTD 2022), examines expectations of decorum, civility, and certainty; and [Imagined Online Communities](https://doi.org/10.1145/3555132) (CSCW 2022) studies how Facebook group admins govern their communities.

topics.intro:
AI systems are increasingly used to inform, judge, and govern — often in ways that reproduce Western assumptions and existing inequalities. We evaluate how large language models behave, examine the politics of the data and methods behind AI, and study how AI is adopted and governed, especially in the Global South.

Our aim is AI that is accountable to the people it affects, grounded in non-ideal, real-world conditions rather than idealized ones.

sections.heading: Evaluating Large Language Models
sections.body:
As LLMs are increasingly used to judge bias, they may themselves show bias in subtler ways. [Evaluating Second-Order Bias of LLMs Through Epistemic Entitlement](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.17506) (EMNLP 2026 Findings) introduces a philosophically grounded way to measure social bias in an LLM's judgments about social bias. We have also tested how LLM-backed chatbots handle [misinformed and demographically informed prompts](https://doi.org/10.1002/aaai.12208) about climate change and mental health (AI Magazine 2025).

We study how people experience these systems in practice: how users flag and respond to LLM sycophancy, a fair, multi-perspective ethical reasoning framework, and [why software engineers sometimes find LLMs counterproductive](https://doi.org/10.1145/3801972) (TOSEM 2026).

sections.heading: Data, Annotation, and Ground Truth
sections.body:
"Ground truth" assumes there is one correct label. [The Consensus Trap](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805689.3806510) (FAccT 2026) reviews five years of research to argue that this paradigm treats human disagreement as noise rather than a vital sociotechnical signal. Annotation is also political: [Data, Annotation, and Meaning-Making](https://doi.org/10.1145/3630106.3659030) (FAccT 2024) shows how annotation overlooks faith-based, religious, and spiritual aspects, drawing on a dataset of faith-based communal violence.

We also look at how AI work gets done. [Towards a Non-Ideal Methodological Framework for Responsible ML](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642501) (CHI 2024) draws on interviews with 22 ML practitioners; Studying People to Study AI (AIES 2026) surveys 93 experts on the place of human research in AI safety and ethics; and [UnWEIRDing Peer Review](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791553) (CHI 2026) examines how review biases disadvantage Global South scholarship.

sections.heading: AI, Power, and Governance
sections.body:
Transparency tools are not neutral. [Bureaucratic Silences](https://doi.org/10.1145/3805689.3812336) (FAccT 2026) analyzes all 409 systems in Canada's first Federal AI Register to show what such registers reveal, omit, and obscure. Prediction Laundering (AIES 2026) examines how prediction markets such as Polymarket produce seemingly objective "truth" that hides uncertainty, manipulation, and capital asymmetries.

In the Global South, we study [Bangladesh's AI readiness](https://doi.org/10.1145/3811242.3819093) across curriculum, infrastructure, and governance (COMPASS 2026), the [ethical risks of computer vision applications](https://doi.org/10.20380/GI2020.17) (GI 2020), and how text-to-image tools reshape creative work — from [the impacts on Bangladeshi image-makers](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3641951) (CHI 2024) to [community-centric design of T2I tools](https://doi.org/10.1609/aies.v8i3.36710) (AIES 2025).

topics.intro:
Behind every digital device is an infrastructure of repairers, recyclers, networks, and workers — much of it informal and invisible, especially in the Global South. We study the knowledge, care, and labour that keep technology working, and the inequalities in who gets connected and on what terms.

Our work ranges from ethnographies of repair shops and e-waste communities to systems that make the web faster in developing regions.

sections.heading: Repair, E-waste, and Care
sections.body:
A six-month ethnography with data repairers in Bangladesh, [Data Repair](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790962) (CHI 2026, Best Paper Honorable Mention), shows how this work is constrained not only by scarce machinery and software but by cross-language learning resources and the protective way repairers document and share their experience. [The Breaking Hand](https://doi.org/10.1145/3290605.3300253) (CHI 2019, Best Paper Honorable Mention) follows the knowledge, care, and suffering of e-waste recyclers in Dhaka, and environmental-health work measured e-waste dismantlers' [exposure to flame retardants](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.137480).

Repair looks different far from cities. [Trust and Technology Repair Infrastructures](https://doi.org/10.1145/3359201) (CSCW 2019, Diversity and Inclusion Award) studies remote fishing and farming villages in the Philippines, and [Pandemic, Repair, and Resilience](https://doi.org/10.1145/3460112.3471965) (COMPASS 2021) documents how COVID-19 disrupted repair and recycling in Bangladesh.

sections.heading: Connectivity and Digital Infrastructure
sections.body:
Mobile broadband is the main way people in the Global South get online, yet its quality is poorly measured. [Measuring the Unmeasured](https://doi.org/10.1145/3789240.3830293) (SIGCOMM 2026 poster) shows how existing measurement renders marginalized communities invisible. [MAML](https://doi.org/10.1145/3696410.3714584) (WWW 2025) works towards a faster web for users on low-end devices and limited bandwidth, whose experience suffers from webpages bloated with third-party CSS and JavaScript.

Infrastructure is social and spatial too. We have studied [privacy vulnerabilities in public digital service centers](https://doi.org/10.1145/3392561.3394642) in Dhaka, the [program and policy landscape for sustainable ICTD](https://doi.org/10.1145/3512973) in Bangladesh, and, in [Others' Images](https://doi.org/10.1145/3313831.3376572) (CHI 2020, Best Paper Honorable Mention), how online fame drives residents to remodel their homes after Western images, with consequences for urban space.

sections.heading: Work and Platforms in the Global South
sections.body:
Platforms reshape work in the Global South in ways that research centred on the Global North can miss. In Bangladesh, Uber car owners are often not the drivers, and [the tensions between them](https://doi.org/10.1145/3449244) (CSCW 2021) shape ridesharing. We have also studied the strategies of [Facebook microcelebrities](https://doi.org/10.1145/3572334.3572368) (ICTD 2022) and how [funders incorporate community voices](https://doi.org/10.1145/3572334.3572402) into development programs (ICTD 2022).

Three years of ethnographic work with internally displaced people in Dhaka's Mohakhali and Kalyanpur areas, [Resilient Hope](https://doi.org/10.1145/3764665) (COMPASS 2025), conceptualizes hope in relation to displacement, marginalization, and resistance.

topics.intro: Health is shaped as much by social, cultural, and economic conditions as by clinical care. We design and study technologies for care in low-resource settings, approaches to mental health that go beyond Western individualistic models, and the barriers that stigma and gender norms create in access to care.

sections.heading: Mobile Care for Children with Autism
sections.body:
Caring for children with autism spectrum disorder is especially challenging in low- and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. [mCARE](https://doi.org/10.1109/COMPSAC48688.2020.0-170) is a mobile-based care system that routinely collects behavioural and developmental data, supporting data-driven decisions by families and practitioners (Pervasive Health 2024). Using mCARE data, we have applied [machine learning to inform developmental milestone achievement](https://doi.org/10.2196/29242) (JMIR Medical Informatics 2021) and studied [patterns of risk and resilience during COVID-19 lockdowns](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-00793-7) (Scientific Reports 2021).

Caregivers also face stigma. Working with 29 parents and nine teachers at special needs schools in Dhaka, ["We Need More Power to Stand Up"](https://doi.org/10.1145/3392561.3394643) (ICTD 2020) designs to combat it at its deeper roots.

sections.heading: Mental Health and Wellbeing
sections.body:
Large language models can personalize support in ways traditional interventions cannot. [Understanding the Role of LLMs in Personalizing and Scaffolding Strategies to Combat Academic Procrastination](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642081) (CHI 2024, Best Paper Honorable Mention) explores what users expect from such tools, and [Perfectly to a Tee](https://doi.org/10.1145/3715336.3735810) (DIS 2025) uses LLMs to tailor stories about overcoming personal struggles, studied with 346 young adults. We also contributed to a [crowdsourced megastudy of 12 digital single-session interventions for depression](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-026-02415-6) (Nature Human Behaviour 2026).

Outside the West, mental health needs different framings. Studying Kaan Pete Roi, a suicide prevention helpline in Bangladesh, ["What's the Point of Having this Conversation?"](https://doi.org/10.1145/3616381) (COMPASS 2023) argues for decolonizing mental health services, and an analysis of 1,000 helpline calls [connects mental health with the Sustainable Development Goals](https://doi.org/10.1145/3572334.3572384) (ICTD 2022).

sections.heading: Access to Care, Gender, and Stigma
sections.body:
Access to care is shaped by stigma, gender norms, and local knowledge. A ten-month ethnography in three villages, [The Ancient Elephant in the Room](https://doi.org/10.1145/3700794.3700797) (ICTD 2024), examines barriers to reproductive care for rural Bangladeshi women, and ["Parar-daktar Understands My Problems Better"](https://doi.org/10.1145/3359270) (CSCW 2019) explores how people in 13 villages access healthcare. [Computing and the Stigmatized](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642005) (CHI 2024, Best Paper Award) studies trust, surveillance, and space with sex workers in Bangladesh, and ["Deprived of support because we're born women"](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791434) (CHI 2026) examines the struggles of women entrepreneurs.

At scale, [From patient voices to policy](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0000739) (PLOS Digital Health 2026) uses natural language processing on over 120,000 patient reviews from 45 Ontario hospitals to surface patterns that can inform policy.
